lessons.title: Context: Youth Violence & Group Psychology
lessons.description: Gang culture, group psychology experiments, and Dennis Kelly’s dramatic style in DNA.
lessons.content_html:
Dennis Kelly and the World of DNA

DNA was first performed at the National Theatre in 2008 as part of the NT Connections programme, which commissions plays specifically for young performers. Dennis Kelly wrote it for teenagers to perform — and about teenagers doing terrible things. The play explores what happens when a group of ordinary young people commit a horrific act of mob violence and then try to cover it up. There is no adult authority in the play: no teachers, no parents, no police officers making things right. The teenagers are entirely alone with the consequences of what they have done.

Kelly has said that the play is about “gangs, genetics and the need to belong.” It asks uncomfortable questions about how far people will go to protect themselves and fit in with a group. The title itself is a double meaning — it refers both to the forensic DNA evidence used in the cover-up and to the deeper question of what is in our nature as human beings. Are we hardwired to follow a leader, even into cruelty?

Key Fact

DNA premiered at the National Theatre in 2008 as part of NT Connections. Dennis Kelly wrote it for young performers, exploring mob violence, group psychology, and the absence of adult authority. The title refers to both forensic evidence and human nature.

Youth Violence and Gang Culture

The play was written during a period of intense public anxiety about youth violence in Britain. In 2007–2008, a series of teenage murders dominated the headlines, and politicians debated “Broken Britain.” Kelly does not set DNA in a specific time or place — there are no street names, no school, no identifiable city. This non-specific setting makes the play feel universal: this could happen in any group, anywhere.

The group in DNA is not a traditional street gang. They are ordinary teenagers who are bound together not by loyalty or friendship but by a shared secret. Once they have committed their crime against Adam, it is guilt and fear — not affection — that holds them together. Kelly shows that a “gang” does not require knives or drugs; it only requires a group of people too frightened to break away.

Kelly uses several distinctive techniques throughout DNA. Dialogue is often fragmented and overlapping — characters interrupt each other, repeat themselves, and leave sentences unfinished. This creates a naturalistic sense of panic and confusion. Stage directions are minimal, giving directors freedom but also reflecting the play’s stripped-back, confrontational style.

Violence is kept offstage throughout. We never see what happens to Adam in the wood; we hear about it through Mark and Jan’s fragmented retelling. This is a deliberate choice. By making the audience imagine the violence rather than watch it, Kelly forces them to become complicit — filling in the horrific details themselves, just as the characters reconstruct and distort what really happened.

The Psychology of Obedience

The behaviour of the group in DNA mirrors real psychological experiments about obedience and conformity. In 1963, Stanley Milgram conducted his famous obedience experiment at Yale University, in which participants were told by an authority figure to deliver electric shocks to a stranger. Sixty-five per cent obeyed to the maximum voltage, even when they believed they were causing serious harm. Milgram concluded that ordinary people will do terrible things when an authority figure tells them to.

Phil functions as the authority figure in DNA. He rarely speaks, but when he does, his instructions are followed without question. “What are you going to do?” the group asks him repeatedly, and whatever Phil says becomes the plan. The group does not challenge him because following orders is easier than taking personal responsibility. Cathy, who volunteers to threaten the postman (Act 2) and involves herself in extreme acts throughout — reflecting Dennis Kelly’s point that ordinary people become capable of violence within a group, is the most extreme example of obedient cruelty — she carries out Phil’s orders with enthusiasm.

Key Fact

Milgram’s obedience experiment (1963) showed 65% of people would obey harmful orders from an authority figure. Phil is the authority in DNA — the group follows his instructions without question, even when those instructions become morally monstrous.

The Stanford Prison Experiment and the Bystander Effect

In 1971, Philip Zimbardo’s Stanford Prison Experiment assigned volunteers to be either “guards” or “prisoners” in a simulated prison. Within days, the guards became sadistic and the prisoners became passive. The experiment had to be stopped early because of the psychological damage. It demonstrated that people adopt the roles they are given — put someone in a position of power and they may abuse it; put someone in a subordinate role and they accept mistreatment.

This maps directly onto DNA. John Tate begins as the group’s leader but cannot cope with the pressure. Phil steps into the power role and becomes increasingly controlling. Cathy, given permission to use violence, escalates rapidly. Meanwhile, the rest of the group — Richard, Danny, Lou — become passive bystanders, unwilling to intervene.

The bystander effect describes how people are less likely to intervene in an emergency when others are present, because each person assumes someone else will act. In DNA, nobody stops the bullying of Adam, nobody refuses Phil’s plan, and nobody goes to the police. Leah is the character who comes closest to moral action — she questions everything, she talks constantly about right and wrong — but even she ultimately fails to act. Her desperate monologues (“You need me”) are directed at Phil, who ignores her, and at an audience who cannot intervene.

Kelly suggests that moral awareness without moral action is meaningless. Leah knows what is right but does nothing, making her complicit. The audience, too, is implicated — we watch and do nothing, mirroring the bystander effect the play dramatises.

Why Context Matters for the OCR Exam

In Component 01, Section A, you may be asked to compare an extract from DNA with an unseen extract from another modern drama. Understanding the social and psychological context of the play — youth violence, obedience, the bystander effect — allows you to analyse Kelly’s intentions (AO3) while examining his use of language and dramatic techniques (AO2). The strongest answers connect specific quotations to broader ideas about human nature and group psychology.
lessons.exam_tip_html: OCR Component 01, Section A has two parts: (a) asks you to compare a DNA extract with an unseen drama extract (20 marks), and (b) asks a broader question about the whole play (20 marks). For part (a), focus on comparing HOW the writers create effects — language, structure, stagecraft — not just WHAT happens. For part (b), use context like Milgram and the bystander effect to show you understand Kelly’s intentions. Always embed context within your analysis rather than adding it as a separate paragraph.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • DNA (2008) explores youth violence and group psychology through a non-specific setting that makes its themes universal — this could happen anywhere.
  • Real psychology experiments — Milgram’s obedience study, the Stanford Prison Experiment, and the bystander effect — directly mirror the group dynamics in the play.
  • Kelly keeps violence offstage and uses fragmented dialogue, forcing the audience to imagine the horror and become complicit in the retelling.

lessons.title: Acts 1-2: The Crime & the Cover-Up
lessons.description: The bullying of Adam, the group’s panic, Phil’s cover-up plan, and Leah’s bonobos speech.
lessons.content_html:
What Happened to Adam

The audience never sees the original crime. Instead, we piece together what happened through Mark and Jan’s fragmented dialogue in the street scenes. The group had been bullying Adam — making him steal vodka, setting his socks on fire, putting a plastic bag over his head. What started as cruel games escalated. They took Adam to a grille in the woods and dared him to walk across it. He fell. They looked down into the darkness and assumed he was dead.

Kelly’s choice to reveal the crime through retrospective narration is crucial. Mark and Jan interrupt each other, contradict each other, and stumble over details. “We were having a laugh,” they insist, as though the word “laugh” can contain what they did. Their fragmented speech mirrors the group’s inability to process the horror — they cannot tell the story straight because they cannot face what it means.

Key Fact

The bullying of Adam escalated from stealing vodka to setting his socks on fire, putting a plastic bag over his head, and finally daring him to walk across a grille. His fall — and the group’s assumption of his death — triggers the entire plot. We learn this only through Mark and Jan’s broken retelling, never through direct action.

Act 1: Panic and Power Vacuum

Act 1 opens in three locations that recur throughout the play: a street (Mark and Jan), a field (Leah and Phil), and a wood (the group). In the street, Mark and Jan establish the crisis. In the field, Leah talks to Phil, who eats an ice cream and says nothing. The stage direction “Phil is eating an ice cream” is one of the play’s most striking images — while everyone else panics, Phil consumes, unmoved. His silence is not confusion; it is the calm of someone who is already thinking.

In the wood, John Tate tries to take charge. He is the group’s nominal leader, but his authority is disintegrating. He bans the word “dead”: “I’m in charge and no one, I’m telling you, no one is going to use that word.” This attempt to control reality through language is both comic and desperate. By forbidding the word, John Tate reveals that he cannot cope with the thing it describes. His leadership is based on denial, and denial cannot hold a group together.

In the field, Leah delivers one of the play’s most important speeches. She talks about bonobos — a species of ape that shares 99.6% of its DNA with humans. Unlike chimpanzees, which are aggressive and hierarchical, bonobos resolve conflict through cooperation and affection. Leah’s point is philosophical: if our DNA is almost identical to a peaceful species, why do humans choose violence?

“We share 99.6% of our DNA with them,” Leah says. “Chimps. Not bonobos. We share more of our DNA with bonobos. But we choose chimps.” This speech is the thematic heart of the play. It connects the title (DNA) to the central question: are humans naturally violent, or do we choose to be? The bonobos represent the road not taken — the peaceful alternative that the group rejects. Phil, characteristically, says nothing in response. His silence forces Leah to talk more, exposing her desperation: “You need me, Phil. Everyone needs someone.”

Phil’s Plan: The Cover-Up

When Phil finally speaks, he takes control instantly. His plan is chillingly methodical. He instructs the group to find a man — any man — and plant Adam’s DNA on him, so the police will arrest an innocent person for Adam’s supposed murder. “We’ve found a man,” the group later reports. Phil’s plan requires the group to steal Adam’s jumper (which has his DNA on it) and leave it near this stranger.

The plan works. A man who lives near the field is arrested. The group has not only covered up their own crime — they have framed an innocent person. Phil shows no remorse. He delivers instructions in short, flat sentences: “Take his jumper. Leave it there. Go home. Say nothing.” The simplicity of his language contrasts sharply with the moral enormity of what he is asking. He breaks complex criminality into manageable steps, making it easier for the group to comply without confronting the full weight of what they are doing.

Key Fact

Phil’s cover-up plan frames an innocent man by planting Adam’s DNA (his jumper) near a stranger. He delivers instructions in short, flat sentences that break criminality into manageable steps, making it psychologically easier for the group to obey without confronting the moral horror of their actions.

Act 2: The Plan in Action

In Act 2, the cover-up is working. The man in the field has been arrested. The group should feel relief, but instead the pressure intensifies. Brian, a minor character, “can’t stop crying.” Cathy is enjoying the drama — she tells the group that a TV reporter has interviewed her about the “missing boy,” and she loved the attention. This is the first sign of Cathy’s dangerous appetite for power and visibility.

Leah, meanwhile, becomes increasingly desperate. In the field, she tries everything to get Phil to respond — talking about chimps and bonobos, threatening to set fire to herself, even attempting it. Phil watches and continues eating. “I’m not saying anything,” he states at one point, as though silence itself is a position. Leah’s monologues become longer and more frantic as the play progresses, revealing that her need for Phil’s acknowledgment mirrors the group’s need for his leadership. Both are forms of dependency.

Each act cycles through three locations: the street (Mark and Jan), the field (Leah and Phil), and the wood (the group). The street scenes function as a chorus, updating the audience on developments. The field scenes explore the personal cost of the crime through Leah and Phil’s dysfunctional relationship. The wood scenes show the group’s collective actions and power dynamics.

By Act 2, the street scenes grow shorter and more tense, the field scenes grow more desperate (Leah’s monologues lengthen), and the wood scenes grow darker as the cover-up deepens. Kelly uses the recurring structure to show escalation: the same locations, but the moral atmosphere gets worse each time we return.

Acts 1 and 2 establish the pattern that defines the play: a crisis occurs, the group turns to Phil, Phil gives orders, the group obeys, and the moral consequences are ignored. Kelly shows that the cover-up is not a one-off decision but a rolling process of deeper and deeper complicity. Each step makes the next one easier to justify and harder to reverse.

Compare HOW the writers create tension, not just WHAT happens. For part (b), track how the cover-up escalates across the play — show you know the whole text, not just the extract.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The crime against Adam is never shown — Mark and Jan’s fragmented retelling forces the audience to piece together the horror, making the violence more disturbing.
  • Phil’s cover-up plan (framing an innocent man with Adam’s DNA) is delivered in cold, flat instructions that break moral enormity into manageable steps.
  • Leah’s bonobos monologue poses the play’s central question: if humans share more DNA with peaceful bonobos than violent chimps, why do we choose violence?

lessons.title: Act 3: Adam Returns
lessons.description: Adam found alive, Phil’s darker orders, Cathy’s violence, and the group fracturing.
lessons.content_html:
The Shocking Reversal

Act 3 delivers the play’s most dramatic twist: Adam is alive. He has been living in a hedge, surviving on scraps, mentally broken but physically present. The boy the group assumed was dead — the boy they built an entire cover-up around — is found by Cathy. This discovery should be good news. Instead, it is the worst thing that could happen to the group, because Adam’s survival threatens the lie that has been holding them together.

Kelly uses this reversal to expose the moral rot at the heart of the group. A living Adam is more dangerous than a dead one, because a dead Adam requires only silence — a living Adam could speak. The group’s first instinct is not relief or joy but fear. “What are we going to do?” becomes the desperate refrain again, and once again all eyes turn to Phil.

Key Fact

Adam’s survival in Act 3 is the play’s central reversal. Rather than bringing relief, it creates a deeper crisis: the group has framed an innocent man, and a living Adam could expose everything. Their response — fear rather than joy — reveals how far they have fallen morally.

Phil’s Darker Orders

Phil’s response to Adam’s reappearance marks a turning point. In Acts 1 and 2, his plan was morally wrong but arguably designed to protect the group. In Act 3, his instructions become explicitly cruel. He orders the group to keep Adam hidden — to take him to a disused building and ensure he never comes forward. “I’ve got nothing to say,” Phil tells Leah when she pleads with him to stop, a line that echoes his earlier silence but now carries a darker weight. His refusal to engage is no longer mysterious; it is wilful detachment.

The group follows Phil’s orders again, but this time the cracks are visible. Richard questions the plan. Lou is uneasy. Even Brian, who has been having a breakdown throughout, seems to recognise that this is different from the original cover-up. Kelly shows that there is a threshold of evil beyond which even passive followers begin to hesitate — but hesitation is not the same as refusal, and nobody actually walks away.

Cathy emerges as the play’s most overtly violent character in Act 3. When Adam is found, she is the one who takes charge of controlling him. She acts with extreme violence and control to prevent Adam from alerting anyone. Cathy’s willingness to harm Adam to ensure silence is the clearest evidence of her moral collapse in the play.

Cathy’s enthusiasm for violence is not reluctant obedience — it is pleasure. She volunteers for the worst tasks and relishes the power they give her. Earlier, she enjoyed being interviewed by a TV reporter about the “missing boy.” Now she enjoys inflicting pain directly. Kelly presents Cathy as a sociopath who has found, in the group’s crisis, the perfect environment for her worst instincts to flourish. Where the Stanford Prison Experiment showed that ordinary people become abusive when given power, Cathy suggests that some people were already waiting for the opportunity.

The Group Fractures

Act 3 is where the group begins to break apart. John Tate, the original leader, has effectively disappeared from the action — his authority shattered. Richard starts to question Phil openly: “Happy? Is that what you are? Happy?” This is the first time anyone directly challenges Phil, and the question is devastating because it suggests Phil may not simply be pragmatic but may be enjoying his control, just as Cathy enjoys her violence.

Danny and Lou remain silent followers, doing what they are told without protest but also without enthusiasm. Brian continues his breakdown. Mark and Jan, the street-scene narrators, report events with increasing detachment, as though they are distancing themselves from what they are describing. Their choral function becomes increasingly ironic: they report atrocities in the same flat tone they used to describe the initial bullying.

Key Fact

Act 3 shows the group fracturing: Richard challenges Phil (“Happy?”), John Tate has vanished, and Mark and Jan report events with increasing detachment. However, nobody leaves the group or goes to the authorities — Kelly shows that awareness of wrongdoing does not equal the courage to act.

Adam barely speaks in Act 3. He has been living rough, surviving alone after his fall. When found, he is described as being in a traumatised state. He is not the same person who walked across the grille — the experience has broken him. Kelly uses Adam’s silence to mirror Phil’s, but where Phil’s silence is power, Adam’s silence is powerlessness. He has no voice, no agency, no ability to help himself. The group treats him as a problem to be managed rather than a person to be saved.

This dehumanisation is one of Kelly’s most disturbing achievements. Adam has gone from a boy who wanted to belong so badly he would endure bullying, to a “living dead” figure who exists only as a threat to the group’s safety. The other characters never ask how he is feeling, what he has been through, or whether he needs help. They ask only: what do we do with him?

Act 3 is the play’s moral nadir. The group has moved from accidental harm to deliberate cruelty, from covering up a death to imprisoning a living person. Phil’s authority has become absolute, Cathy’s violence has been unleashed, and Leah’s moral objections have been completely ignored. The audience watches the last traces of decency drain away from the group, replaced by the cold logic of self-preservation at any cost.

For the whole-text essay (part b), track the escalation from Acts 1–2 into Act 3, showing how Phil’s orders become darker and Cathy’s violence moves from offstage to onstage. Richard’s “Happy?” is a key quotation for exploring the theme of complicity.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Adam’s survival is a reversal that worsens the crisis — a living witness is more dangerous than a dead victim, revealing how far the group has fallen.
  • Cathy’s torture of Adam with a cigarette is the play’s most violent moment, showing her evolution from enthusiastic follower to active sadist.
  • The group fractures but nobody leaves — Kelly shows that recognising evil is not the same as having the courage to resist it.

lessons.title: Act 4: The Ending
lessons.description: Phil’s withdrawal, Leah’s disappearance, Cathy as leader, and the play’s moral collapse.
lessons.content_html:
Act 4: A World Without Conscience

Act 4 is the shortest act in DNA, and its brevity is part of its power. Kelly does not provide a satisfying resolution. Instead, the final act shows the aftermath of moral collapse — a world where the characters who tried to do right have vanished and the characters who embraced cruelty have inherited control. The audience is left not with catharsis but with unease.

The act opens, as always, in the street with Mark and Jan. But the information they deliver is devastating. Phil has withdrawn completely. Leah has gone — “she’s gone,” Jan says simply, with no further explanation. The two characters who occupied the field scenes — the play’s moral and intellectual centre — have been erased from the story. The audience never learns where Leah went or why. This deliberate ambiguity is one of Kelly’s most unsettling choices.

Key Fact

By Act 4, Phil has withdrawn into silence, Leah has disappeared, John Tate has “found God,” and Cathy has become the group’s new leader. Kelly shows that moral collapse is not dramatic — it happens quietly, as decent people give up and cruel people fill the vacuum.

Phil’s Withdrawal

Phil does not face justice or experience a dramatic downfall. He simply stops. In the field scene of Act 4, he sits alone. There is no ice cream, no Leah chattering beside him. Richard arrives and tries to talk to him, but Phil says nothing. The structural echo of the earlier field scenes is devastating: where once Phil’s silence was power, now it is emptiness. He has controlled, manipulated, and commanded, and now he has nothing left.

Kelly leaves Phil’s state deliberately ambiguous. Is he consumed by guilt? Has he simply run out of problems to solve? Has his emotional shutdown finally become permanent? The text offers no answers. Phil’s silence, which once made him the most powerful character in the play, now makes him the most pitiable. He has achieved nothing except destruction, and the group he controlled has moved on without him.

Leah’s disappearance is one of the play’s most haunting elements. She spent the entire play talking — about bonobos, about happiness, about whether Phil needed her. “You need me,” she insisted. “Everyone needs someone.” But Phil never responded, never acknowledged her, never gave her the connection she craved. By Act 4, she has simply gone.

Kelly does not tell us whether Leah left voluntarily, broke down, or something worse. Her absence is a narrative gap that forces the audience to confront the consequences of being the moral voice that nobody listens to. If conscience is constantly ignored, it eventually falls silent. Leah’s disappearance is the logical conclusion of the bystander effect: when nobody responds to your pleas, you stop making them.

Cathy as the New Leader

With Phil withdrawn and Leah gone, Cathy steps into the power vacuum. Mark and Jan report that she has taken charge of the group, and the implications are terrifying. Cathy was the character who enjoyed violence, who relished the TV interview, who tortured Adam with a cigarette. She represents the play’s worst-case scenario: a leader who is not merely amoral (like Phil) but actively sadistic.

Kelly traces a clear leadership succession: John Tate (weak, denial-based) is replaced by Phil (effective, amoral) who is replaced by Cathy (violent, sadistic). Each leader is worse than the last. This declining trajectory is Kelly’s bleakest commentary on group dynamics: without external moral authority, power gravitates towards whoever is willing to be the most ruthless.

Key Fact

The leadership succession — John Tate (denial), Phil (amorality), Cathy (sadism) — shows power becoming more dangerous at each stage. Kelly suggests that without moral checks, leadership will always gravitate to the most ruthless person in the group.

Richard’s Unanswered Plea

The play’s final scene is Richard visiting Phil in the field. He tries to talk to him, asks him questions, tells him what has happened. Phil says nothing. Richard’s final line — a desperate, unanswered appeal — echoes Leah’s earlier monologues. Richard has become Leah: the person who talks to Phil and receives only silence. The cyclical pattern suggests nothing has changed, nothing has been learned, and the same dynamics will repeat.

Kelly offers no redemption. There is no confession, no punishment, no reconciliation. The framed man presumably remains in prison. Adam is presumably still hidden. And the group continues, led now by its most dangerous member. The ending refuses the audience the comfort of closure, leaving them with the disturbing implication that this kind of moral collapse is not exceptional — it is ordinary, quiet, and ongoing.

Mark and Jan reveal the fates of other group members. John Tate has “found God” — he has turned to religion, which could be read as genuine repentance or as another form of denial, swapping one authority figure for another. Brian, who spent the play in emotional collapse, is described as being on medication. Danny and Lou have faded into the background, their passivity now permanent.

These scattered fates reinforce Kelly’s message: the group has not been brought to justice. Some members have coped through denial (John Tate), some through chemical numbness (Brian), some through new allegiances (following Cathy). Nobody has confronted what they did. The absence of justice is Kelly’s final, most disturbing statement.

The ending of DNA is deliberately unsatisfying. Kelly denies the audience the traditional dramatic resolution where wrongs are righted and the guilty are punished. Instead, the play ends with silence, absence, and the quiet triumph of cruelty over conscience. It is this refusal of comfort that makes DNA such a powerful and haunting piece of modern drama.

Focus on the leadership succession (John Tate → Phil → Cathy) and the cyclical structure (Richard replacing Leah in the field). The absence of justice is a key AO3 point — Kelly deliberately refuses redemption to make the audience uncomfortable.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Act 4 offers no resolution: Phil withdraws, Leah disappears, and Cathy — the most violent character — becomes the new leader.
  • The leadership succession (John Tate → Phil → Cathy) traces a declining moral trajectory, with each leader worse than the last.
  • Richard’s unanswered plea to Phil mirrors Leah’s earlier monologues, creating a cyclical structure that implies nothing has been learned.

lessons.title: Character Analysis
lessons.description: Phil, Leah, John Tate, Cathy, Richard, Adam, and Mark and Jan as chorus.
lessons.content_html:
Phil: The Silent Controller

Phil is the most powerful character in DNA, yet he speaks less than anyone. For much of the play, he sits in a field eating — an ice cream in Act 1, a muffin in Act 2, chips in Act 3. These recurring motifs of consumption make Phil appear absurdly calm while chaos surrounds him. His silence is not ignorance; it is control. When the group panics and asks “What are you going to do?” Phil waits, thinks, and then delivers instructions with chilling precision.

Phil’s plans are always effective. He frames an innocent man in Acts 1–2, orchestrates Adam’s imprisonment in Act 3, and in each case the group obeys without question. But Kelly never reveals Phil’s inner life. We do not know if he feels guilt, satisfaction, or nothing at all. “I’ve got nothing to say,” he tells Leah — and this opacity is what makes him so disturbing. He may be a calculating manipulator or a teenager so emotionally shut down that cruelty comes without feeling. By Act 4, Phil has withdrawn entirely — his silence now emptiness rather than power.

Key Fact

Phil controls the group through silence and minimal speech. His calm eating while others panic, his cold instructions (“Take his jumper. Leave it there. Go home. Say nothing.”), and his refusal to engage emotionally make him the play’s most powerful and most opaque character. By Act 4, this silence has become emptiness.

Leah: The Moral Conscience

Leah is Phil’s opposite: she never stops talking. Her monologues about bonobos, happiness, and the nature of friendship are the play’s most philosophical passages. She poses the central question — “We share more of our DNA with bonobos. But we choose chimps” — and she is the only character who consistently questions whether the group’s actions are right. She threatens to set fire to herself to provoke a response from Phil, revealing the depth of her desperation for his acknowledgment.

Yet Leah never acts. She knows what is right but does not go to the police, does not refuse to participate, does not leave the group. “You need me,” she tells Phil, but he does not. Kelly presents Leah as proof that moral awareness without moral courage is useless. Her disappearance in Act 4 — unexplained, abrupt — is the logical consequence of a conscience that nobody listens to. She represents the audience’s own discomfort: we see the wrong but do not intervene.

John Tate is the group’s first leader, and his failure sets the pattern for everything that follows. When news of Adam’s apparent death reaches the group, John Tate tries to take charge through denial and intimidation. He bans the word “dead”: “I’m in charge and no one is going to use that word.” But controlling language does not control reality, and his authority collapses as the group recognises he has no plan.

John Tate’s weakness creates the vacuum that Phil fills. If John Tate had been a competent leader, the group might have confessed or found a less destructive solution. Instead, his collapse demonstrates that leadership based on bluster rather than competence will always fail under pressure. By Act 4, John Tate has “found God” — swapping one form of authority for another, still unable to think for himself.

Cathy: The Sociopath

Cathy is the play’s most overtly dangerous character. While others follow Phil’s orders reluctantly, Cathy follows them with enthusiasm. She enjoys being interviewed by a TV reporter about the “missing boy.” She volunteers to threaten the postman. She tortures Adam with a cigarette. Each act of cruelty is escalation, and Kelly makes clear that Cathy was never coerced — she was waiting for permission. By Act 4, she has replaced Phil as leader, completing the play’s darkest trajectory.

Richard, Adam, and the Chorus

Richard is the closest the group has to an everyman figure. He is uncomfortable with the cover-up, anxious, and in Act 3 challenges Phil directly: “Happy?” But he never leaves or acts on his discomfort. In Act 4, he takes Leah’s position in the field, talking to a silent Phil — the cycle repeating. Richard shows that doubt without action changes nothing.

Adam is the play’s absent centre. He is talked about constantly but barely appears. When he does, he is silent and broken. Kelly presents him as the ultimate victim — first bullied, then assumed dead, then imprisoned when found alive. The group treats him as a problem, never as a person. His silence contrasts with Phil’s: where Phil chooses silence, Adam has had his voice taken from him.

Mark and Jan function as a modern Greek chorus. They appear in the street scenes, finishing each other’s sentences and relaying information to the audience. Their dialogue is fragmented and rapid — they interrupt and overlap, creating a breathless sense of urgency. They are not major decision-makers but narrators who report what has happened.

Kelly uses Mark and Jan to control the audience’s access to information. We learn about Adam’s bullying, the cover-up, and the group’s fate through their reports. Their increasing detachment as the play progresses — reporting atrocities in the same tone they used for gossip — mirrors the group’s moral numbness. They are also complicit, because reporting events without condemning them is its own form of silence.

Key Fact

Kelly’s characters represent different responses to moral crisis: Phil (control without conscience), Leah (conscience without action), John Tate (denial), Cathy (sadistic enthusiasm), Richard (discomfort without courage), Adam (dehumanised victim), and Mark and Jan (detached narration). Together they map the full spectrum of complicity.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For both parts of the OCR exam, character analysis is essential. In part (a), compare how Kelly presents a specific character trait (e.g. power, silence, moral awareness) with how the unseen writer does the same. In part (b), the strongest essays analyse characters as representatives of ideas — Phil as amoral power, Leah as impotent conscience, Cathy as unleashed sadism — rather than simply describing what they do.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Phil controls through silence and minimal speech; Leah represents conscience without action — together they embody Kelly’s argument that power and morality have been divorced.
  • The leadership succession (John Tate → Phil → Cathy) shows each leader becoming more dangerous, with power gravitating to the most ruthless.
  • Mark and Jan function as a Greek chorus, and their increasing detachment mirrors the group’s moral numbness.

lessons.title: Structure & Stagecraft
lessons.description: Four-act structure, three locations, paired characters, offstage violence, and Leah’s monologues.
lessons.content_html:
The Four-Act Structure

DNA is divided into four acts, each cycling through three locations: a street, a field, and a wood. This cyclical structure gives the play its distinctive rhythm. Each time we return to a location, the situation has worsened. The street scenes grow more tense, the field scenes more desperate, and the wood scenes more dangerous. Kelly uses this repetition to show escalation: same places, but the moral temperature drops each time.

The four acts are not equal in length. Acts 1 and 2 are the longest, establishing the crime and the cover-up. Act 3 is shorter but more intense, delivering the reversal of Adam’s survival. Act 4 is the shortest — a compressed, devastating coda that shows the aftermath. This structural contraction mirrors the group’s moral collapse: as their humanity shrinks, so does the play.

Key Fact

Each act cycles through three locations: street (Mark and Jan as chorus), field (Leah and Phil’s relationship), and wood (group decisions). The acts get progressively shorter as moral collapse accelerates, with Act 4 as a brief, devastating coda.

The Three Locations

Each location serves a distinct dramatic purpose. The street is where Mark and Jan deliver exposition. They function as a Greek chorus, updating the audience in fragmented, overlapping dialogue. The street represents the public face of the crisis — the version of events that the outside world might see.

The field is Leah and Phil’s space. It represents the private, emotional dimension of the crisis. Here, Leah delivers her philosophical monologues — about bonobos, about happiness, about whether Phil needs her — while Phil eats and says nothing. The field is where introspection happens, though it is one-sided: only Leah reflects.

The wood is where the group meets and where Phil delivers his orders. It represents the collective — the space where group decisions are made and individual morality is overridden. The wood is also where Adam fell, giving it a symbolic weight as the scene of the original crime. Kelly’s choice to have the group return to the wood for their deliberations is darkly ironic: they keep returning to the place of their guilt.

Kelly structures the play around character pairs. Mark and Jan are always together, finishing each other’s sentences. Leah and Phil are always together in the field, their dysfunctional relationship playing out in parallel with the group’s crisis. Even in the wood, characters tend to operate in pairs or small clusters rather than as a unified group.

This pairing creates contrasts that illuminate the play’s themes. Phil’s silence is thrown into sharp relief by Leah’s speech. Mark and Jan’s shared narration contrasts with the isolation of characters like Brian (who breaks down alone) and Richard (who questions alone). Kelly uses these structural pairings to show that even within a group, people are fundamentally isolated by their different responses to moral crisis.

Offstage Violence

One of Kelly’s most distinctive choices is to keep nearly all violence offstage. The bullying of Adam, his fall, the framing of the innocent man, and much of Cathy’s violence are described rather than shown. We hear about them through Mark and Jan’s reports or through the group’s panicked discussions, but we do not witness them directly.

This technique serves several purposes. First, it makes the violence more disturbing, because the audience’s imagination fills in details that are worse than anything staging could show. Second, it implicates the audience in the retelling — just as the characters reconstruct and distort what happened, the audience must reconstruct it from fragments. Third, offstage violence keeps the focus on the characters’ responses rather than on the acts themselves — Kelly is less interested in what happened than in what people do afterwards.

Key Fact

Kelly keeps violence offstage to make it more disturbing (the audience imagines worse), to implicate the audience in reconstruction, and to focus on the characters’ responses rather than the acts themselves. This is a key AO2 point about dramatic method.

Leah’s Monologues as Dramatic Device

Leah’s monologues are the play’s philosophical spine. They are long, rambling, and apparently disconnected from the main plot — she talks about bonobos, about chimps, about whether happiness is real, about the nature of friendship. But each monologue connects thematically to the group’s crisis. The bonobos speech asks why humans choose violence over peace. The happiness speech asks whether the group can ever recover from what they have done. The friendship speech asks what it means to need someone who does not need you.

These monologues are delivered to Phil, who never responds. This creates a unique form of dramatic monologue — not a soliloquy (Phil is present) but not a dialogue (Phil does not reply). Leah is simultaneously speaking to Phil, to herself, and to the audience. Her increasing desperation — the monologues get longer and more frantic as the play progresses — mirrors the group’s moral disintegration. When she finally disappears in Act 4, the play loses its conscience, and the audience feels the absence.

Kelly’s stage directions are minimal and functional. He does not describe elaborate sets or detailed blocking. The most famous stage direction — “Phil is eating an ice cream” — is powerful precisely because of its simplicity. It tells us everything we need to know about Phil’s character in seven words.

This minimalism gives directors enormous freedom in staging the play. It also reflects Kelly’s focus on language and character over spectacle. The play can be performed with almost no set — three playing areas, a few props — and this stripped-back quality makes it ideal for young performers (its original NT Connections purpose) while also concentrating the audience’s attention on what the characters say and do not say.

In part (b), discuss how the shortening acts mirror moral collapse, how the cyclical structure shows nothing changes, and how Leah’s monologues function as philosophical commentary that the other characters ignore.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The three locations (street, field, wood) each serve a distinct purpose: public narration, private emotion, and collective decision-making.
  • Offstage violence forces the audience to imagine the horror, making them complicit; it also keeps the focus on the characters’ responses.
  • Leah’s monologues are the play’s philosophical spine — apparently random but thematically connected, and increasingly desperate.

lessons.title: Language & Silence
lessons.description: Phil’s silence as power, Leah’s verbal desperation, euphemism, and fragmented dialogue.
lessons.content_html:
Silence as the Most Powerful Language

In most plays, the characters who speak the most hold the most power. In DNA, the opposite is true. Phil barely speaks, yet he controls everything. His silence is not passive — it is an active strategy of control. By refusing to speak, Phil forces the group to come to him, to beg for instructions, to depend on him. The repeated question “What are you going to do?” shows that Phil’s silence creates a vacuum that only he can fill.

When Phil does speak, his words are devastatingly effective. His instructions are short, flat, and imperative: “Take his jumper. Leave it there. Go home. Say nothing.” There is no emotional language, no justification, no persuasion. He does not explain why his plan is necessary; he simply states what must be done. This minimal directive language makes his orders feel inevitable rather than debatable. The group complies because Phil’s speech style removes the option of discussion.

Key Fact

Phil’s silence is not absence but strategy. When he does speak, his flat, imperative sentences (“Take his jumper. Leave it there. Go home. Say nothing.”) remove the possibility of debate and make criminal actions feel like simple instructions to be followed.

Leah’s Verbal Desperation

Leah is the opposite of Phil: she fills every silence with words. Her monologues are long, rambling, and increasingly frantic. She talks about bonobos: “We share 99.6% of our DNA with them.” She talks about happiness: “Are you happy? Is that what you are?” She talks about friendship: “You need me, Phil. Everyone needs someone.” Each monologue is an attempt to provoke a response from Phil, and each one fails.

Kelly uses Leah’s speech as a form of verbal filling. The more Phil refuses to respond, the more Leah talks. Her language becomes a mirror of her emotional state: as her desperation increases, her sentences become longer, more repetitive, more fragmented. She jumps between topics, circles back, contradicts herself. This linguistic disintegration tracks the group’s moral disintegration — as things fall apart, so does coherent speech.

The group’s language is full of euphemism. Mark and Jan describe the bullying as “having a laugh.” The group refers to Adam’s fall as “what happened.” John Tate bans the word “dead.” Phil’s instructions avoid naming the crime: he says “take his jumper” and “leave it there,” not “plant evidence to frame an innocent man.”

This linguistic avoidance is a form of moral distancing. By refusing to name what they have done, the characters create a buffer between themselves and the truth. If they do not say “murder” or “torture” or “frame,” then perhaps those things are not really what they did. Kelly shows that language is not just a tool for communication — it is a tool for self-deception. The group lies to itself through the words it chooses and the words it avoids.

Fragmented Dialogue and Interruption

Much of the dialogue in DNA is fragmented. Characters interrupt each other, leave sentences unfinished, and talk over one another. Mark and Jan’s street-scene dialogue is the clearest example — they share sentences, each picking up where the other left off, creating a breathless, anxious pace:

“MARK: So we were —
JAN: Having a laugh.
MARK: Having a laugh, we were, and —
JAN: He fell.”

This shared dialogue serves several purposes. It creates naturalism — real teenagers speak in fragments, especially under stress. It creates urgency — the overlapping rhythm makes events feel chaotic and out of control. And it shows that Mark and Jan are so enmeshed in the group that they cannot even narrate independently; their identities have merged into a single choral voice.

Key Fact

Kelly uses language in four key ways: Phil’s silence as control, Leah’s verbal desperation as failed conscience, euphemism as moral distancing, and fragmented dialogue as naturalism and urgency. Each technique reveals character and theme simultaneously.

“I’m Not Saying Anything” — The Paradox of Speech

Phil’s line “I’m not saying anything” is one of the play’s richest paradoxes. By saying he is not saying anything, he is saying something. He is declaring his position: silence is his chosen stance. This line encapsulates the play’s exploration of communication and its failures. Phil communicates through absence. Leah communicates through excess. The group communicates through euphemism and fragmentation. Nobody in DNA says what they actually mean, and this failure of honest communication is both a symptom and a cause of the moral breakdown.

Throughout the play, sentences are left incomplete. Characters trail off, change direction mid-thought, or are interrupted before they can finish. This is not careless writing — it is a deliberate representation of the unsayable. The things the group has done are so terrible that language itself breaks down. They cannot describe the bullying without euphemism. They cannot discuss Adam without evasion. They cannot name the moral horror because naming it would force them to confront it.

Kelly suggests that language fails when moral reality becomes too uncomfortable to articulate. The gaps in the dialogue — the pauses, the unfinished sentences, the things not said — are where the real meaning lives. An attentive audience reads the silences as carefully as the speech.

In part (b), discuss how Phil’s directive language makes criminal acts feel like simple instructions, and how Leah’s verbal filling mirrors the group’s moral disintegration.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Phil’s silence is a strategy of control: by refusing to speak, he creates a vacuum that only he can fill, making the group completely dependent on him.
  • Euphemism (“having a laugh,” banning the word “dead”) is a form of moral self-deception that allows the group to avoid confronting what they have done.
  • Fragmented, overlapping dialogue creates naturalism and urgency while showing how the group’s identities have merged under stress.

lessons.title: Key Themes & Exam Technique
lessons.description: Guilt, leadership, peer pressure, morality, silence, and OCR comparison technique.
lessons.content_html:
Theme: Guilt and Responsibility

Guilt is the engine that drives DNA. Every character responds to it differently, and Kelly uses these varied responses to explore the full spectrum of moral failure. Phil suppresses guilt through emotional shutdown — he eats, stays silent, and treats the crisis as a logistical problem. Leah expresses guilt through her monologues, talking incessantly about bonobos and happiness as though philosophical reflection can substitute for moral action. Cathy appears to feel no guilt at all, relishing the excitement of the cover-up and the violence that follows.

The play’s most important insight about guilt is that responsibility is diffused across the group. Nobody feels individually accountable because they all participated together. John Tate bans the word “dead” to avoid confronting guilt. Brian breaks down but does not confess. Richard questions Phil but does not leave. Kelly shows that collective guilt is more dangerous than individual guilt, because within a group, everyone can convince themselves that someone else is really to blame.

Key Fact

Kelly presents guilt as something the group diffuses rather than confronts. Each character avoids responsibility differently: Phil through silence, Leah through talk, Cathy through enthusiastic participation, John Tate through denial, Brian through breakdown, and Richard through unanswered questions.

Theme: Leadership and Power

The leadership succession in DNA — John Tate to Phil to Cathy — is one of its most important structural patterns. John Tate leads through bluster and denial, which collapses under pressure. Phil leads through silence and cold efficiency, which is effective but amoral. Cathy leads through violence and intimidation, which is the play’s endpoint of moral deterioration.

Kelly suggests that without external moral authority (there are no adults in the play), leadership gravitates to whoever is willing to be the most ruthless. The group does not choose its leaders consciously; leaders emerge because they fill the vacuum created by the previous leader’s failure. This is a deeply pessimistic view of power dynamics — it implies that in any group, given enough pressure, the cruellest person will eventually take charge.

Peer pressure operates on two levels in the play. On the surface, it drives the bullying of Adam — each member of the group participates because the others do, and nobody wants to be the one who refuses. Below the surface, it drives the cover-up. Once Phil devises his plan, the group follows because the social cost of refusal — isolation, exposure, being the outsider — feels worse than the moral cost of complicity.

Adam is the play’s most extreme victim of peer pressure. He endured bullying because he wanted to belong: he stole vodka, ate leaves, walked across a grille, all because the group told him to. His desperation to fit in led directly to his fall. Kelly presents a devastating irony: Adam’s need to belong is what destroys him, and the group’s need to hold together after his fall is what destroys their morality.

Theme: Silence and Complicity

Silence takes many forms in DNA. Phil’s silence is strategic power. Adam’s silence is imposed powerlessness. The group’s silence (nobody goes to the police) is complicity. Leah talks endlessly but might as well be silent, because nobody listens. The play argues that silence is not neutral — choosing not to speak when something is wrong is itself a moral choice, and a damning one.

Kelly extends this to the audience. We watch the play, we see the horror unfold, and we do nothing — because we cannot. But the discomfort we feel is exactly the point. Kelly wants us to recognise that we, too, are bystanders. The play’s lack of resolution — no confession, no punishment, no redemption — refuses to let us off the hook. We leave the theatre as complicit in our inaction as the characters in theirs.

Key Fact

The five key themes of DNA are: guilt and responsibility (diffused across the group), leadership and power (declining succession), peer pressure (drives both bullying and cover-up), silence and complicity (choosing not to act is a moral choice), and morality (conscience without action is useless).

Exam Technique: The Comparison Question

Your paper may give you an extract from DNA alongside an unseen extract from another modern drama or prose text and ask you to compare how both writers present a theme, character type, or dramatic effect. Treat this as a comparative analysis task, with language, structure and context all under test. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact question wording, mark weighting and recommended timing.

The key to a strong comparison is comparative analysis — not writing about one text then the other, but weaving them together. Use connecting phrases: “Similarly, the unseen writer uses…” “In contrast, Kelly presents this through…” “Both writers use fragmented dialogue, but where Kelly’s creates panic, the unseen writer’s creates…”

A whole-text question asks a broader question about DNA as a whole. Plan to cover at least three moments from different parts of the play, showing you know the text from beginning to end. Structure your response around the question’s key concept (e.g. leadership, violence, silence) and use well-chosen evidence including precise quotations.

For AO1, make clear points about the play’s meaning. For AO2, analyse Kelly’s methods — his use of silence, fragmented dialogue, offstage violence, the three locations, the leadership succession. For AO3, embed relevant context: the 2008 premiere, youth violence, Milgram, the Stanford Prison Experiment, the bystander effect. The best essays integrate all three assessment objectives within each paragraph, not in separate sections.

A strong essay on DNA will argue that Kelly’s play is not about one group of teenagers but about human nature itself. The non-specific setting, the universal themes, and the deliberate refusal of resolution all point to a writer who believes that the potential for moral collapse exists in every group and every individual. The question is not whether it will happen, but what we do when it does.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For part (a), always compare methods, not just content. Use linking phrases (“Similarly,” “In contrast,” “Both writers”) to weave the texts together. For part (b), cover at least three moments from across the play and integrate AO1 (meaning), AO2 (methods), and AO3 (context) within each paragraph. Quote precisely and analyse at word level — e.g. why “laugh” in “having a laugh” is a euphemism that reveals moral self-deception.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The five key themes — guilt, leadership, peer pressure, silence/complicity, and morality — are interconnected: each theme reinforces the others throughout the play.
  • For part (a), weave the texts together using comparative connectives rather than writing about one text then the other.
  • For part (b), integrate AO1, AO2, and AO3 within each paragraph, covering at least three moments from across the play.
